facts.statement: Qianosuchus is an extinct aquatic archosaur from the Middle Triassic of Pan County, China.
facts.quote: Qianosuchus is an extinct genus of aquatic poposauroid archosaur from the middle Triassic (Anisian) Guanling Formation of Pan County, China.

facts.statement: Qianosuchus was more than 3 meters long.
facts.quote: Qianosuchus was more than 3 metres long

facts.statement: The genus is known from three nearly complete skeletons and a crushed skull.
facts.quote: Es conocido a partir de tres esqueletos casi completos y un cráneo aplastado.

facts.statement: Qianosuchus was described by Li C. et al. in 2006.
The type species of Qianosuchus is Q. mixtus.
facts.quote: subdivision: * Q. mixtus Li C. et al., 2006 (type)

facts.statement: Qianosuchus belongs to the order Paracrocodyliformes.
Qianosuchus is classified within the superfamily Poposauroidea.
The upper jaw had nine long teeth in each premaxilla and eighteen teeth in each maxilla.
facts.quote: Each premaxilla has nine long teeth, and the maxillae bear eighteen teeth each.

facts.statement: All of Qianosuchus's teeth were laterally compressed, curved backwards, and serrated.
facts.quote: All the teeth are laterally compressed, curved backwards and serrated, like those of most other carnivorous archosaurs.

facts.statement: A specimen described in 2023 showed that the lower jaw possessed 22 teeth on each side.
facts.quote: The dentary turns down very slightly at the tip; a specimen described in 2023 shows that it possessed 22 teeth on each side of the lower jaw.

facts.statement: Each orbit contained a large scleral ring that would have reinforced the eyeball under pressure during diving.
facts.quote: Each orbit had a large and well-developed scleral ring in it, which would have reinforced the eyeball under pressure when Qianosuchus was diving.

facts.statement: The neural spines grew taller towards the rear of the tail, making the caudal vertebrae tall.
facts.quote: The neural spines grow taller posteriorly (further down the tail), making the caudal vertebrae tall.

facts.statement: Qianosuchus had very small, numerous osteoderms located only on the top of the neck and torso.
facts.quote: The osteoderms are very small and numerous, and they are only present on top of the neck and torso, precluding their subsequent disappearance in later poposauroids.

facts.statement: The forelimbs were slender, lightly built, and almost totally straight, with diminutive metacarpals and manual phalanges.
facts.quote: The forelimbs were slender and lightly built, and almost totally straight, and the specimen described in 2023 shows diminute metacarpals and manual phalanges

facts.statement: Qianosuchus could walk on land with an erect or semi-erect posture based on its ankle joint.
facts.quote: However, its pelvic girdle and large, relatively unspecialized legs would have allowed Qianosuchus to walk around on land as well, and may well have had an erect or semi-erect posture, based on the ankle joint.

facts.statement: Qianosuchus likely lived a semi-aquatic lifestyle, hunting in or on shallow seas and on land.
facts.quote: All this suggests that Qianosuchus lived a semi-aquatic lifestyle in and around the shallow seas where it lived, hunting either on water or on land.

facts.statement: Qianosuchus lived during the Anisian stage of the Middle Triassic in the Guanling Formation of Pan County, China.
facts.quote: from the middle Triassic (Anisian) Guanling Formation of Pan County, China.

facts.statement: Qianosuchus possessed long, slender hyoid bones with slightly expanded ends.
facts.quote: The hyoid bones are long and slender, with slightly expanded ends.
